title: A Teen Taught Himself to Fly Stolen Planes
central_question: How did a runaway teenager with no known flight training steal at least five planes, fly one to the Bahamas, and how did it end?
content_notes: Remarkable and ironic, never glamorising theft and never mocking his childhood or poverty. Colton Harris-Moore is alive; he served his sentence and was released, and nothing is said about his life now. He appears only as a faceless silhouette tagged NOT A LIKENESS. No weapon is drawn or mentioned; no one is hurt on screen (the crash-landed plane is empty, the boat chase shows only lights on the water). The shop owner, deputies, Bahamian officers and the plane owner are generic figures, never named; no badge, crest, flag, logo, aircraft registration or real business name is drawn. His self-teaching is attributed ('Reportedly'). The statistic card names its source and years. Every card is our own typed graphic. No dialogue is invented. Status verified 2026-10-15.

lines.text: And he left his bare footprints behind.
At one shop, he even drew them in chalk.
How did a teenager learn to fly?
He reportedly used manuals and flight simulator games.
He took at least five planes. Three crashed.
In Indiana, he stole one more,
and flew over 1,000 miles to the Bahamas.
A week later, a boat chase ended it.
For teenagers, burglary arrest rates fell over 90 percent.
Own a plane, boat or cabin? Save these three.
He got over seven years and left prison in 2016.
His movie deal repaid victims over a million dollars.

claims.text: The first plane he is believed to have stolen was a Cessna 182 (Skylane) owned by a Seattle radio host, taken from Orcas Island Airport, Washington, in November 2008. Narration: 'At 17, he started stealing planes.'

Born 22 March 1991 (Wikipedia); described as 18 in October 2009 (AVweb) and 19 at his capture in July 2010 (AP). He was therefore 17 in November 2008 when the first plane was taken. The AGE chip reads 17 (2008), 18 (2009), 19 (2010).
Bare footprints at several crime scenes earned him the nickname 'Barefoot Bandit' (earlier 'Barefoot Burglar'). Narration: 'And he left his bare footprints behind.'
His two-year run began after he walked away from a halfway house (group home) in April 2008.

He hid out and committed most of the crimes around Washington State's islands: Camano Island (where he grew up) and the San Juan Islands (Orcas Island). Narration: 'A runaway, he hid out in Washington's islands.'

In February 2010 at a grocery store on Orcas Island (his second break-in there), he drew cartoonish bare feet in chalk on the floor (CBS: 39 footprints; count not used). Narration: 'At one shop, he even drew them in chalk.'
FUN FACT CARD: next to the chalk feet leading out of the door he wrote 'C-YA!' (ABC spells it 'c yah'). Card: 'HE DREW CHALK BARE FEET / AND WROTE "C-YA!"'.
REPORTED / BELIEVED: he had no known formal flight training and is believed to have learned to fly from aircraft manuals, a 'how to fly' DVD and flight-simulator computer games. .
AOPA: no known formal flight training. Headline: 'TAUGHT HIMSELF TO FLY' (CBS: 'taught himself how to fly').
He stole at least five planes (CBS: 'five private planes'; AOPA: 'at least five').

Three of them were crash-landed / destroyed or badly damaged (CBS: 'crash-landing three of them'; AOPA: destroyed or badly damaged three). Example: the Cessna 182 taken from Bonners Ferry, Idaho, on 29 Sept 2009, crash-landed near Granite Falls, Washington, after running out of fuel; he walked away unhurt.
Over the 4 July 2010 weekend he took a 2009 Cessna 400 (Corvalis) from a pried-open hangar at Monroe County Airport, Bloomington, Indiana.

He flew it more than 1,000 miles (AP: 'more than 1,000 miles'; Herald-Times about 1,100; NBC about 1,200) and crash-landed it in marshy water / a mangrove swamp on Great Abaco, Bahamas, on 4 July 2010. Narration: 'and flew over 1,000 miles to the Bahamas.'

A week later, before dawn on 11 July 2010, Bahamian police caught him off Eleuthera (reported as Harbour Island / northern Eleuthera) after a high-speed boat chase in a stolen boat; police disabled the boat's motor. (He threw a gun into the water; not shown or mentioned.) Narration: 'A week later, a boat chase ended it.'
He was 19 at his capture.

STATISTIC (counter): the under-18 (juvenile) burglary arrest rate fell 93 % from its 1980s average to 2020, while the adult rate fell 69 %; by 2020 the two rates were about the same (Council on Criminal Justice burglary fact sheet, July 2024, from OJJDP Statistical Briefing Book data). OJJDP's 'Juvenile Arrests, 2019' independently reports juvenile burglary arrest rates at their lowest since at least 1980, and 'Juvenile Arrests 2004' a 70 % fall from 1980 to 2004. Narration: 'For teenagers, burglary arrest rates fell over 90 percent.' (the card gives the years)

LESSON CARD (practical): do not leave or hide keys in or around the aircraft/hangar (AOPA) or a spare house key outside (LA County Sheriff); add an auxiliary/second lock (AOPA: throttle, prop or prop-control locks; LASD: dead-bolt locks); report anyone suspicious or lurking (AOPA Airport Watch 'Lock up, look out'; Ramsey County Sheriff). Rows: 'NEVER HIDE A SPARE KEY', 'ADD A SECOND LOCK', 'REPORT ANYONE LURKING'.

State: pleaded guilty to some 30 counts in Island County Superior Court; sentenced 16 Dec 2011 to 7 years 3 months (AVweb; AP 'more than 7 years'). Federal: pleaded guilty 17 June 2011 to seven charges incl. interstate transportation of stolen aircraft; sentenced 27 Jan 2012 to 6 1/2 years, concurrent with the state term. Narration: 'He got over seven years'.

In September 2016 Washington's Department of Corrections moved him from prison to Reynolds Work Release in Seattle; he was later released from work release, under supervision. Narration: 'and left prison in 2016.' (Sentence served; nothing is said about his life now.)

His plea deal required that proceeds from any movie or book deal go to restitution; 20th Century Fox bought the film rights (reported up to $1.3 million) and by late 2015 had paid more than $1 million towards court-ordered restitution to his victims (largest single cheque $900,000). Narration: 'His movie deal repaid victims over a million dollars.'
